newsitem.title: USA: Minn. gov to call session for education funding.
newsitem.headline: Minn. gov to call session for education funding.

text.p: Minnesota Gov. Arne Carlson announced late Monday that he will call a special session to resolve an impasse over education funding for the upcoming fiscal biennium.

Carlson, who advocates tax credits for private school tuition, announced that he would veto the education spending plan approved by lawmakers near the close of their session on Monday because it contains no significant reform to help students failing basic skills tests.

"The legislature has had five months to put together a bill which will help the growing percentage of children who are failing," Carlson said in a prepared statement. "I am disappointed to report tonight (Monday) that they were unable to accomplish that goal."

Minnesota lawmakers approved an approximately $22 billion budget for the next two years at midnight Monday that includes more than $750 million of property tax cuts and additional tax credits, said Tom Smalec, spokesman for the house leadership.
Legislative leaders were also discussing on Tuesday a response to Carlson's plans for a special session, Smalec said.

The spending plan also includes some debt issuance, less than $100 million, Smalec said. Minnesota approves most of its capital projects in non-budget years, when debt issuance runs from $500 million to $600 million on average, he said.
The tax package includes a one-time $500 million property tax rebate and rate reductions for various types of commercial, industrial and rental housing, Smalec said.

The property tax rebate approved will be payable as a refundable income tax credit on 1998 state income tax returns, Smalec said. It applies for homeowners, renters and the homestead portions of farms, he noted.
Legislators also approved a $157 million a homestead education credit program to protect homeowners and farmers from the effect of lowering property tax rates on other properties, Smalec said.
Also increased the statewide education levy about $30 million to shift the net impact on the state contribution to public school instruction from 60 percent to almost 70 percent, Smalec said.

Legislators also imposed levy limits on counties and cities for the next two years, but included exemptions for cities with fewer than 2,500 residents and communities that sustained flood damage this year, Smalec said.
Minnesota fiscal analysts have predicted that the state will have a $2.3 billion budget surplus at the end of the fiscal biennium in 1999, Smalec said.
Lawmakers also approved $970 million of spending for public safety issues, Smalec said.
Carlson has not yet set a date to begin the session.
